new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no existing statement for waha1238, so this is the first stress datum: final stress in citation forms, evidenced by the transcriptions rather than by a stated rule. It matches what Blust 2017 (already held by the project, fn. 11 p.198) says for the WESTERN Lowland Kenyah villages Long Sela'an/Long Ikang/Long San ('Stress was invariably recorded as final in citation forms'), and the same notebook's Long San pages (pp. 124-125, scan 062, viewed: ta'ʔdʲaw, la'ʔun, mə'ʔdʲuk, ma'ʔdʲit) use the identical final-tick convention, so the 1971 notebook is the fieldnote basis of that footnote and extends it to Long Dunin. new_statements.rule_in_words: The notebook contains no prose statement about stress. But in the Long Dunin (Uma' Pawa') wordlist (pp. 127-137) every polysyllabic citation form that carries Blust's stress tick has it before the last syllable (tu'suʔ, pi'ʔən, puu'luʔ, uu'suʔ, kaa'viŋ, taa'kət, maa'sat, dʲaa'nan, ñaa'tuŋ, muu'iʔ, sii'gut, aa'nit, lii'kut, baa'tək, aa'tay, puu'suʔ, tii'sən, taa'kut, uu'ləw, baa'tuk, ba'ʔuʔ, jii'pən, taa'wɛ; p.132 uu'ban, daa'law, tuu'sap, təə'baw; p.134-135 paa'kuʔ, sii'ləw, sii'kəw, suu'kup, kaa'saŋ, kəda'yay, səmi'ləw, jəlu'tuŋ), including trisyllables (kalu'nan, pəpa'tay, nəmu'tun, ñəma'yaw, məŋa'mɛt, kətən'nəʔ). No form is marked with non-final stress; many short/unmarked forms carry no tick at all. Stress therefore falls on the final syllable in citation forms; the long penultimate vowels (taa-, puu-, sii-) are not stressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing; no secondary marks anywhere in the section.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The only phonological notes in the section are 'Note: both pronunciations are used and accepted as correct when given' (p.129, about variant forms), 'Note: b, d are imploded' (p.132) and 'Note: n is dental' (p.136). Two forms are given with a syllabification note ('luu'nduʔ (syllabification is lu.nduʔ)', p.128). Whether the placement holds in phrasal context is not addressed (Blust 2013:186 notes that some Sarawak languages have final stress in citation but penultimate in phrase).
new_statements.identity_note: The notebook describes Long Dunin on the Tinjar river, Sarawak (Malaysia), whose people 'call themselves Uma' Pawa'' and 'moved from the Belaga river in 1960' (p.127). Blust 2017 fn. 2 treats Long Dunin = Uma' Pawa' as a close relative of Lebu' Kulit and leaves it unclassified; Glottolog's waha1238 'Eastern Lowland Kenyah' (Ethnologue whk Wahau Kenyah, Kalimantan) is the node that groups Lebu' Kulit and Uma' Pawe (Smith 2017 used Uma' Pawe of Long Apu). The identification of this Sarawak Uma' Pawa' community with waha1238 therefore rests on the Uma' Pawa'/Uma' Pawe ethnonym and Blust's Lebu' Kulit link, not on a source that names the glottocode. Data are from one speaker (Jonas Lian) and a single session on 28 Sept 1971.
